content.title: Adding Supporting Details
content.overview: This lesson focuses on selecting the sentence that best strengthens a paragraph's central idea. Success requires identifying the main claim and choosing a detail that provides concrete evidence, examples, or effects rather than introducing new topics or repeating information.
learning_objectives: Identify the central idea of a paragraph in a single phrase.
Distinguish between relevant supporting details and off-topic distractors.
Select sentences that provide concrete evidence, statistics, or examples to bolster a claim.
Verify that a chosen detail maintains the paragraph's focus without shifting the topic.

sections.title: Identifying the Central Idea
sections.content: Before looking at the answer choices, you must determine the paragraph's 'Central Idea.' This is the primary claim or focus the author is trying to communicate. Ask yourself: 'What is the one thing this paragraph is trying to prove or describe?' Summarize this in a short phrase. Every sentence in a well-written paragraph should serve this central idea.

sections.title: The Support-by-Function Strategy
sections.content: When the ACT asks which sentence 'best supports' or 'strengthens' a point, use the Support-by-Function strategy. First, identify the main claim. Second, eliminate distractors that introduce new, unrelated topics or simply repeat what has already been said. Third, look for the 'Goldilocks' detail: a sentence that provides a concrete example, a specific effect, or a relevant statistic that directly illustrates the main idea.

sections.title: Recognizing Distractor Traps
sections.content: ACT distractors for this topic usually fall into three categories: 1) Irrelevant New Topics: Information that is interesting but unrelated to the specific claim. 2) Tangential Facts: Information that relates to a word in the paragraph but not the paragraph's purpose. 3) Repetition: Restating the main idea in different words without adding new evidence or depth.

worked_examples.question:
Context: City planners proposed converting a vacant lot into a community garden to improve neighborhood well-being. The project aims to increase access to fresh produce and create communal green space. [INSERT SENTENCE HERE] The plan includes volunteer shifts and a small educational garden for local schools.

Which sentence, if inserted, best supports the paragraph’s main idea?
A) The garden would host monthly workshops demonstrating how to grow vegetables in small spaces.
B) The lot has been empty for years because developers lacked funding for any projects.
C) The mayor once said he liked community art installations during a ribbon-cutting ceremony.
D) A survey showed that 78% of nearby residents said they would use a community garden weekly.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Identify the central idea. The paragraph is about how a community garden will improve neighborhood well-being through produce and green space. Step 2: Evaluate choices. Choice B (funding) and Choice C (mayor's art preference) are new topics that don't support 'well-being.' Choice A describes a specific activity (workshops), which is related but doesn't prove the garden's impact. Step 3: Select the best evidence. Choice D provides a concrete statistic (78% usage) that directly supports the claim that the garden will improve the neighborhood by showing high resident engagement. Correct Answer: D.

common_mistakes: Choosing a sentence just because it is 'true' or 'interesting' even if it doesn't support the specific main idea.
Selecting a sentence that repeats the main idea instead of providing new evidence for it.
Picking a detail that shifts the focus to a sub-topic or a different subject entirely.
exam_tips: Look for concrete nouns and numbers; statistics and specific examples are often stronger support than general statements.
If two choices seem relevant, pick the one that is more specific to the claim made in the first two sentences of the paragraph.
Always perform a 'Final Check': Read the paragraph with your chosen sentence included to ensure the flow remains logical and focused.
content.recap: To add the best supporting detail, identify the paragraph's main claim and select the option that provides concrete evidence, such as a statistic or specific example. Avoid choices that repeat the claim or introduce unrelated topics.

knowledge_claims.content: The central idea is a one-phrase summary of a paragraph's main claim or primary focus.
The first step in selecting a supporting detail is to identify the paragraph's main idea in a short phrase before reading the options.
Supporting details are sentences that provide evidence, examples, or clear effects directly tied to the central idea.
A common distractor is a sentence that introduces a new topic unrelated to the paragraph's main claim.
Avoid choices that merely repeat existing facts or restate the main idea without adding new evidence.
Concrete examples, statistics, and specific effects are preferred over general statements when strengthening a claim.
The final check for a supporting detail is to confirm it links to the main idea without shifting the focus to a different claim.
A sentence describing a program's activities is often less supportive than a sentence providing evidence of that program's impact or success.
Tangential facts are distractors that relate to a specific word in the text but do not support the paragraph's overall purpose.
In the Support-by-Function strategy, you must eliminate options that shift the topic away from the neighborhood or subject benefits defined in the main idea.
Specific evidence (like a survey result) is stronger support for a claim of 'well-being' than a general statement about a leader's preferences.
When evaluating choices, cross out options that are factually true but topically irrelevant to the specific paragraph goal.

items.stem:
Practice form 1. Rina is editing a short report about a community garden.

Which sentence would best support the claim that the revision worked?
A) The labels were printed on white paper.
B) One volunteer owned a bicycle.
C) After the labels were added, completed checkouts increased from 18 to 31 per week.
D) The director arrived before noon.

options.A: The labels were printed on white paper.
options.C: After the labels were added, completed checkouts increased from 18 to 31 per week.

items.explanation: The correct choice directly applies the target skill: 添加最能支持中心的细节.

videoLesson.title: Select the Best Supporting Detail
videoLesson.description: Recognize the paragraph’s main idea and compare sentences for topical fit. Eliminate new-topic or repetitive choices and pick a concrete example or effect.
